$comment: V-13, the other half: Scala and Rust must name the same file the same way.
Each case builds a small tree under a fresh temp root, canonicalizes `input`
(relative to that root), and expects `expect` (also relative to the root,
after the root itself has been resolved). Expressing both sides relative to
a resolved root is what makes these assertions platform-independent: on
macOS /tmp is a symlink to /private/tmp, and an absolute expectation would
be testing that rather than the rule.
Where a platform genuinely differs, the difference is WRITTEN DOWN rather
than discovered: `expectCaseInsensitive` applies on macOS and Windows,
`expect` on Linux. P0 established that the case-insensitive filesystem is
the majority case, not the edge case (D2.1b).
The rules being pinned, from gx-core's FileOrigins.canonicalize:
1. a relative path resolves against the caller's cwd, not the process's
2. an existing path becomes its real path — symlinks resolved
3. a path that does NOT exist yet still gets a stable identity: normalize
it, then real-path the deepest ancestor that does exist and re-attach
the remainder. v1's Rust instead fell back to the raw absolute path, so
`..` and unresolved symlinks survived into policy checks
4. on Windows the \\?\ verbatim prefix is stripped, because Java's
toRealPath does not produce one and the two sides must agree

canonicalization.name: a symlinked directory resolves to its target
a symlinked file resolves to its target
V-07: a symlink escaping upward is resolved before any policy check
canonicalization.$why: this is the entire substance of V-07 — a link inside an allowed root pointing outside it is an allowed path naming a denied file, and only resolution first catches it

canonicalization.name: a file that does not exist yet still gets a stable identity
a not-yet-created file under a symlink resolves through it
canonicalization.$why: the case v1's Rust got wrong: canonicalize fails on a missing file, and it fell back to the raw path with the symlink unresolved

canonicalization.name: dot segments in a not-yet-created path are still resolved
a case variant follows the filesystem, and both languages follow it the same way
canonicalization.$why: macOS and Windows report INSENSITIVE and resolve to the on-disk spelling; Linux is sensitive, so A.DOT is simply a different, not-yet-existing file
